description: English writing, grammar and editing conventions.

entries.text: Clear English: one idea per sentence, active voice ('the script reads the file' not 'the file is read by the script'), concrete nouns, verbs that carry the meaning.
Cut padding: 'in order to' → 'to', 'due to the fact that' → 'because', 'at this point in time' → 'now', 'utilise' → 'use'. Delete 'very', 'really', 'basically', 'just'.
Common confusions: its (possessive) / it's (it is); their / there / they're; affect (verb) / effect (noun); fewer (countable) / less (mass); who (subject) / whom (object); lose / loose.

Punctuation: comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two full sentences; semicolon joins two related sentences without a conjunction; colon introduces a list or explanation; em dash for an aside.
Paragraphs: lead with the point, then support it; 3-5 sentences; one topic each. Readers skim first sentences, so make them carry the argument.
Emails: subject states the ask or outcome; first line says what you need and by when; details below; sign off plainly. Formal register = no contractions, full sentences, no slang.

Fiction: show state through action and dialogue rather than labelling emotions; keep point of view consistent within a scene; vary sentence length for pace; cut adverbs on dialogue tags ('said' is enough).
When asked to rewrite or proofread: return the corrected text first, then a short list of the changes and why. Keep the author's voice; do not rewrite meaning.
Definitions: give the meaning in one plain sentence, one example sentence, and the part of speech; note register (formal/informal/technical) when it matters.
Technical writing: define a term the first time you use it, then use that exact term consistently; prefer numbered steps for procedures and tables for comparisons.
